title: From three TI alumni to NASDAQ in seven years
body:
## The founding thesis

In November 2017, three engineers from Texas Instruments walked out of the semiconductor industry's then-dominant analog and embedded franchise and started a company premised on an observation that looked, at the time, closer to speculation than product roadmap: that PCIe and CXL connectivity silicon would become the rate-limiting layer of next-generation server architectures. The three founders — Jitendra Mohan, Sanjay Gajendra, and Casey Morrison — had arrived at TI by a shared route. Mohan and Gajendra had both spent years at National Semiconductor, the analogue house that TI absorbed in 2011, before folding into the combined entity. Mohan, a BTech from IIT Bombay and MS from Stanford EE, had been at National Semi from 1996 through 2011 ending as a design director, then remained at TI through 2017. Gajendra, with an MEng from Colorado-Boulder, had run a broadly parallel arc — Wipro from 1996, National Semi from 2006, TI from 2014. The shared formation was not incidental. National Semiconductor's design discipline — analogue precision, signal-integrity rigour, low-power budgets — was the operational DNA that would later show up in Astera's gross-margin structure.

The company incorporated in Santa Clara. Mohan took the CEO seat. Gajendra became President and COO. Morrison, whose public profile was less extensive than his co-founders', became Chief Product Officer. The foundational bet was that hyperscalers and AI-server OEMs would need purpose-built connectivity silicon as PCIe generations compressed — a market that incumbent vendors serving the broader server ecosystem were structurally slow to address.

## Capital formation and governance architecture

The Series A was led by Sutter Hill Ventures, the Palo Alto firm with a specific record in infrastructure software and silicon. Stefan Dyckerhoff, the Sutter Hill partner, joined the Astera board in 2019. The subsequent funding rounds brought in Fidelity, GlobalFoundries Ventures, and Intel Capital, assembling a cap table that included both strategic and institutional visibility. The presence of Avigdor Willenz Group was a particular signal: Willenz, the founder of Galileo Technology (acquired by Marvell in 2001) and Annapurna Labs (acquired by Amazon in 2015), represented a form of connectivity-silicon pattern recognition that was rare among venture investors. Willenz's involvement was the link to Manuel Alba's board appointment. Alba joined as Chairman in March 2018 — months after the company was incorporated — giving Astera governance infrastructure earlier than most Series A-stage companies acquire it.

The board construction through 2022 continued the same methodical logic. Michael Hurlston — who would become CEO of Lumentum, a position he still held at the snapshot date — joined in 2022. Jack Lazar, a former CFO of GoPro with the kind of public-company financial discipline that audit committees require, joined in December 2022. Each addition layered a specific capability: Alba for M&A and connectivity market navigation, Dyckerhoff for venture-capital cycle awareness, Hurlston for operating-company perspective in adjacent optical and connectivity markets, Lazar for audit-grade financial governance.

## Product architecture: four families, one thesis

Through 2018 to 2023, Astera built four distinct product families without deviating from its foundational connectivity-silicon thesis. Aries covered PCIe and CXL retimers — the signal-conditioning chips that allow PCIe lanes to traverse longer distances inside a rack without degradation, the most immediate commercial application. Taurus addressed Ethernet smart cable modules. Leo targeted CXL memory controllers. Scorpio extended the portfolio into PCIe and CXL fabric switches, a move into the rack-scale topology layer.

Engineering centres in Israel — led by SVP Guy Azrad — and Bangalore — led by SVP Shivananda R. Koteshwar — deepened the technical capacity. The Israel operation gave Astera access to the deep signal-integrity talent concentrated in that ecosystem; the India centre anchored software and verification capacity. Together they allowed the company to execute across multiple product generations simultaneously without running the kind of concentrated engineering risk that single-site startups carry.

By late 2022 and into 2023, design-ins at hyperscalers and AI-server OEMs were converting into revenue visibility. FY2023 delivered $115.8 million in revenue, up 45 per cent year-on-year — proof of commercial traction, though the number that mattered more was what the pipeline implied about FY2024.

## The IPO: priced into an inflection

Astera Labs priced its NASDAQ IPO on March 20, 2024 at $36 per share, above the initial $32 to $34 range — itself a signal that book demand exceeded supply at the lower price. The shares opened for trading at $52.56, a 71 per cent premium to the offering price. The stock closed the first day near $62, implying an enterprise value that had moved from approximately $9.5 billion at the IPO price to north of $13 billion by the close of trading. For a seven-year-old connectivity-silicon company that had reported $115.8 million of revenue in its most recent fiscal year, the reception reflected investor conviction that the AI infrastructure buildout would require exactly the kind of purpose-built retimer and connectivity silicon Astera had spent six years designing in.

The timing was precise. The IPO landed as hyperscaler capital expenditure on AI infrastructure was accelerating toward what would become the defining secular trend of the decade. Astera had not manufactured that timing; it had simply arrived at the IPO window with the right product at the right moment in the PCIe 6.0 and early-CXL adoption curve.

## The first public year: 242 per cent and GAAP profitability

FY2024 produced $396.3 million in revenue, a 242 per cent increase from FY2023's $115.8 million. The gross margin settled in the low 70s per cent on a GAAP basis. The more structurally significant outcome was that Astera became GAAP-profitable during 2024 — an unusual result for a venture-funded silicon company in its first full year of public reporting. The explanation was mechanical: 242 per cent revenue growth landing against an engineering cost base that had been built to absorb considerably more scale produced operating leverage that compressed the loss profile and then flipped it into profit. The company had not engineered its way to profitability through restructuring or cost discipline in the conventional sense. It had simply grown faster than its fixed costs.

Bethany Mayer joined the board in June 2024, adding HPE-era network infrastructure depth and experience from Box and Lam Research.

## The structural-margin year: FY2025

FY2025, covered in the 10-K filed on February 26, 2026, was the year in which Astera's margin profile became the story as much as its growth rate.

| Metric | FY2024 | FY2025 | Change |
|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| Revenue (USD M) | 396.3 | 852.5 | +115% |
| GAAP gross margin | ~72% | 75.7% | ~+370 bps |
| GAAP net income (USD M) | — | 219.1 | — |
| Non-GAAP net income (USD M) | — | 331.0 | — |
| Operating cash flow (USD M) | — | 319.3 | — |
| Liquid balance sheet (USD M) | — | 1,187.6 | — |

Revenue reached $852.5 million, up 115 per cent year on year. The 75.7 per cent GAAP gross margin placed Astera in the top decile of fabless semiconductor companies on that metric — a level associated with software economics rather than silicon. Q3 2025, reported October 28, 2025, was the company's first quarter above $200 million. Q4 2025, reported February 24, 2026, was the first above $250 million at $270.6 million — up 92 per cent year-on-year and 17 per cent sequentially. Q1 2026 guidance of $286 to $297 million implied continued sequential growth.

The $1.19 billion liquid balance sheet — $167.6 million in cash and $1.02 billion in marketable securities against essentially no debt — was the other structural fact of the year. It gave Astera the capacity to absorb a multi-quarter AI capex pause, execute a targeted acquisition, or ramp next-generation tape-outs without near-term financing risk.

## Leadership continuity and the CFO succession

In March 2025, Craig Barratt joined the Astera board. Barratt carried a Stanford EE PhD and a resume that ran through Atheros Communications as CEO, Qualcomm Atheros as President, Barefoot Networks as CEO, and Intel's Connectivity Group. He was simultaneously serving on the Intel board of directors, where he had been designated incoming Chairman effective May 13, 2026. The dual appointment — to one of the most consequential US semiconductor companies at a critical juncture in its recovery and to Astera at the same moment — was widely read as a signal of how tightly Astera's connectivity-silicon stack was expected to integrate with the server platform transition that Intel was navigating.

Mike Tate, the CFO who had taken the company through its IPO and first public years, retired effective March 2, 2026, with transition services extending through September 1, 2026. His successor, Desmond Lynch, arrived from Rambus, where he had served as SVP Finance and CFO from 2022 through 2026. The Rambus background was noted: Lynch had managed a business structured around IP licensing and royalty economics — a model built on defending and monetising a tight portfolio of high-margin assets. The appointment telegraphed continued focus within Astera on the IP-and-margin architecture of its product mix.

## The seven-year arc

A company founded by three engineers from a Texas Instruments hallway in November 2017 reached $852 million of annual revenue at 75.7 per cent GAAP gross margin within seven years of incorporation and within two years of being public. That trajectory — from Series A thesis to structural-margin profitability and a fortress balance sheet — is the seven-year arc. The board assembled over that period was not constructed for IPO execution alone; each appointment after Alba's 2018 chairmanship added a specific layer of capability for the governance challenges that come after the IPO. The question facing Astera at the snapshot date was the same one facing every connectivity-silicon vendor at a generational inflection: whether design-in position at the Nvidia Rubin and AMD MI400-series generation could be secured on terms that preserved the margin structure that made the preceding two years remarkable.
